title: Git and GitHub Workflows for Teams
subtitle: Use Git with confidence on a team: clean commits, branches and merges, pull requests and reviews on GitHub, releases, and a way back from any mistake.
outcomes: Record work in small, well-described commits, and find answers in the history with log, show, diff and blame
Branch, merge and rebase with confidence, and resolve merge conflicts
Collaborate through remotes: fetch, pull and push, recover from rejected pushes, and share branches
Run a team workflow on GitHub with pull requests, code review, protected branches and a consistent merge method
Mark releases with semantic version tags and GitHub Releases, and patch old versions with cherry-pick
Undo mistakes safely with restore, reset, revert and the reflog, and automate checks with Git hooks
prerequisites: None beyond using a terminal: changing folders and running commands, as taught in Linux Command Line Essentials. Python Programming with PyCharm shows Git inside an IDE; this course goes further, on the command line and on GitHub. You need Git 2.28 or later (on Windows, Git for Windows, which includes Git Bash), a text editor, a free GitHub account, and the GitHub CLI (gh) for modules 3 and 4.
description:
Git is how software teams keep track of every change and work on the same code without getting in each other's way. This course starts with what Git records and how to make clean, focused commits, then teaches branching, merging, resolving conflicts and rebasing on the command line, so you understand what the buttons in any tool are doing. You'll practise with remotes by playing two team members on one computer, then move to GitHub: pull requests, code review with suggestions, CODEOWNERS and protected branches, GitHub flow compared with trunk-based development, the three merge methods, and tagged, semantically versioned releases.

Every module has a lab in real repositories, some created for you by small scripts: a café menu with branches to merge and rebase, a shared remote with two clones, and a repository whose history needs repairing. The last module covers .gitignore, undoing almost anything with restore, reset, revert and the reflog, and automating checks with Git hooks. The capstone brings it all together in a small team project on GitHub, from the first commit to a release and a patch. Afterwards, CI/CD and Automated Testing builds automated pipelines on top of this workflow.

modules.title: Commits and history
modules.summary: How Git records a project: the working tree, the staging area and commits; how to make small commits with clear messages; and how to search and read the history they build.

lessons.title: How Git records your work
objectives: Explain the working tree, the staging area and commits
Configure Git and make your first commit
Read git status to see the state of each file
key_points: Git keeps a project's history in a repository, the hidden .git folder at the project's top level. The working tree is the files you see and edit, and the staging area (also called the index) holds what will go into the next commit.

A commit is a snapshot of the whole project at one moment, with its author, date, message and a link to the commit before it, its parent. Following the parents from the newest commit walks back through the history.
Each commit is named by a hash of its contents: a 40-character hexadecimal ID, which commands accept shortened to its first seven or so characters. Changing anything about a commit gives it a new ID.

git status lists files as untracked (new to Git), modified or staged. git add copies a file's current changes into the staging area, and git commit -m "message" records everything staged as a new commit.

Before your first commit, set your name and email with git config --global user.name and user.email: they are written into every commit. git config --global init.defaultBranch main makes new repositories start on a branch called main.

steps.do: Check that Git is installed (2.28 or later), then tell it who you are and what to call the first branch. On Windows, use Git Bash.
steps.code:
git --version
git config --global user.name "Sam Taylor"
git config --global user.email "sam@example.com"
git config --global init.defaultBranch main
steps.see: git version 2.x; the config commands print nothing.

steps.do: Make a folder for the project and turn it into a repository.
steps.code:
mkdir recipes
cd recipes
git init
steps.see: Initialized empty Git repository in .../recipes/.git/

steps.do: Create a README (in your editor, or with printf as here) and ask Git what it sees.
steps.code:
printf '# Recipes

Family recipes, tested and written down.
' > README.md
git status
steps.see: On branch main, No commits yet, and README.md listed under Untracked files.

steps.do: Stage the file and check again.
steps.code:
git add README.md
git status
steps.see: README.md under Changes to be committed, as new file:   README.md.

steps.do: Commit it with a message.
steps.code: git commit -m "Add a README"
steps.see: [main (root-commit) 445633f] Add a README and 1 file changed, 3 insertions(+). Your hash will differ: it depends on the content, your name and the time.

steps.do: Look at the history in full, then one line per commit.
steps.code:
git log
git log --oneline
steps.see: The full 40-character ID, Author: Sam Taylor <sam@example.com>, the date and the message; then 445633f Add a README.

lessons.title: Making good commits
objectives: Check what will be committed with git diff and git diff --staged
Stage part of a file with git add -p
Write clear commit messages, and fix the last commit with --amend
key_points: A good commit makes one logical change, such as one bug fix or one small feature, with everything it needs and nothing else. Small, focused commits are easier to review, to understand later and to undo.
git diff shows the changes you haven't staged; git diff --staged shows what is staged, which is exactly what the next commit will contain. Checking it before each commit catches stray edits.

git add -p (patch mode) shows each change, called a hunk, in turn and asks whether to stage it: y for yes, n for no, s to split a hunk into smaller ones. Unrelated changes in one file can then go into separate commits.
A commit message starts with a summary line of about 50 characters, written as a command (Fix the login timeout, not Fixed it), then a blank line and a body that explains why the change was needed.

git commit --amend replaces the last commit with a new one, adding whatever is staged and letting you change the message. Amend only commits you haven't pushed: the result is a different commit, with a new ID.

git commit without -m opens an editor for the message. Choose it with git config --global core.editor, such as "nano" or "code --wait" for Visual Studio Code; otherwise Git may open Vim, which you leave by pressing Esc and typing :wq.

## Ingredients

- 100 g plain flour
- 2 eggs
- 300 ml milk
- 1 tbsp oil
- a pinch of salt

## Method

1. Whisk the flour, eggs and milk into a smooth batter.
2. Heat the oil in a frying pan.
3. Pour in a ladle of batter and cook for 1 minute on each side.

steps.see: (1/2) Stage this hunk [y,n,q,a,d,j,J,g,/,e,?]? after the first hunk, then (2/2) Stage this hunk after the second.

git commit -m "Use 120 g of flour in pancakes"

git commit -m "Rest the batter" -m "Resting lets the flour soak up the milk, which gives lighter pancakes."

steps.code:
git commit --amend -m "Rest the pancake batter for 10 minutes" -m "Resting lets the flour soak up the milk, which gives lighter pancakes."
git log --oneline
steps.see: Four commits, the newest now Rest the pancake batter for 10 minutes, with a new hash.

lessons.title: Reading history
objectives: Search and filter history with git log
Inspect a commit with git show, and name commits relative to HEAD
Find who last changed a line, and when, with git blame
key_points: git log lists commits newest first. --oneline shows one line per commit, --graph draws the shape of branches and merges, --stat lists the files each commit changed, and -p shows the full changes.
Filter history to what you need: --author="Sam", --since="2 weeks ago", a path after -- for commits that touched one file, and -S "text" (the pickaxe) for commits that added or removed that text.
git show <commit> displays one commit's message and changes. HEAD means the commit you're on, HEAD~1 its parent and HEAD~2 the commit before that, so recent commits don't need a hash.
git blame <file> shows, for every line, the commit, author and date that last changed it; -L 10,20 limits it to those lines. It points you to the commit whose message should explain the line.
git diff A B compares any two commits or branches, and --stat summarises the comparison by file. Clear commit messages make all of these tools more useful, because the why is stored next to the what.

steps.do: Show the history as a graph, one commit per line.
steps.code: git log --oneline --graph
steps.see: * a158fde Rest the pancake batter for 10 minutes at the top, then the three older commits.

steps.code: git log --stat -1
steps.see: The full message, body included, and pancakes.md | 5 +++--.

steps.code: git log -S "120 g" --oneline
steps.see: 9f7a678 Use 120 g of flour in pancakes

modules.title: Branches, merging and rebasing
modules.summary: Work on several things at once with branches, bring work together with fast-forward and three-way merges, resolve conflicts calmly, and keep history tidy with rebase and interactive rebase.

lessons.title: Branches and HEAD
objectives: Explain what a branch and HEAD are
Create, switch between and delete branches
Recognise a detached HEAD and leave it safely
key_points: A branch is a movable label that points at a commit. When you commit on a branch, its label moves forward to the new commit, so branches are cheap: each is just a name for a line of work.
HEAD tells Git where you are: normally it points at the current branch, and new commits go on that branch. git branch lists the branches, with * beside the current one.

git switch -c name creates a branch at the current commit and switches to it (older guides use git checkout -b); git switch name moves to an existing branch and updates the files to match. Commit your changes before switching.

Short, descriptive branch names, such as fix/login-timeout or add-export, tell the team what each branch is for. git branch -d name deletes a merged branch; -D forces it, and its unmerged commits are then lost from view.

git switch --detach <commit> (or checking out a tag) gives a detached HEAD: HEAD points at a commit rather than a branch, so new commits there belong to no branch. git switch - goes back; git switch -c name keeps any work done there.

steps.do: List the branches.
steps.code: git branch
steps.see: * main

steps.do: Create a branch for a new recipe and switch to it.
steps.code: git switch -c add-waffles
steps.see: Switched to a new branch 'add-waffles'

steps.do: Add a waffle recipe and commit it on the branch.
steps.code:
printf '# Waffles

- 250 g self-raising flour
- 2 eggs
- 400 ml milk
' > waffles.md
git add waffles.md
git commit -m "Add a waffle recipe"

steps.do: See every branch in the graph.
steps.code: git log --oneline --graph --all
steps.see: The waffle commit on top, labelled (HEAD -> add-waffles), with main pointing at the commit below it.

lessons.title: Merging
objectives: Explain fast-forward and three-way merges
Merge a branch and read the result in the graph
Delete branches once they're merged
key_points: git merge name brings another branch's commits into the current branch. If the current branch hasn't moved since the other one started, Git simply moves its label forward: a fast-forward merge, with no new commit.
If both branches have new commits, Git makes a three-way merge: it compares each branch with their merge base, the last commit they share, and records a merge commit with two parents.

Since Git 2.34 the default merge strategy is called ort, so Git reports Merge made by the 'ort' strategy (older versions say 'recursive'). git merge --no-ff makes a merge commit even when a fast-forward was possible.
git log --oneline --graph shows a merge as lines that split and join again. A merge commit's default message is Merge branch 'name', and Git opens your editor to confirm it unless you pass --no-edit.
After merging, delete the branch with git branch -d name: its commits stay in the history, reachable from main. Git refuses to delete with -d a branch whose commits aren't merged anywhere.

walkthrough.title: A fast-forward, then a real merge

steps.do: On main, merge the waffle branch.
steps.code: git merge add-waffles
steps.see: Updating a158fde..791f22d, then Fast-forward and waffles.md | 5 +++++.

steps.do: Delete the merged branch.
steps.code: git branch -d add-waffles
steps.see: Deleted branch add-waffles (was 791f22d).

steps.do: Start a crêpe branch and commit a recipe on it, then go back to main and change the README, so both branches move on.

- 125 g plain flour
- 2 eggs

lessons.title: Resolving merge conflicts
objectives: Explain when and why a merge conflict happens
Read conflict markers and resolve a conflict
Abort a merge, and show the common ancestor with zdiff3
key_points: A conflict happens when both branches changed the same lines, or one changed lines the other deleted, since their merge base. Git merges everything else, stops, and leaves the conflicting part for you to decide.

git status lists conflicted files under Unmerged paths as both modified. In the file, the lines between <<<<<<< and ======= are your side (HEAD), and those between ======= and >>>>>>> come from the branch being merged.
To resolve, edit the file to what it should be, delete every marker line, then git add the file and run git commit (or git merge --continue). The result can be one side, the other, or a combination.
git merge --abort gives up and puts everything back as it was before the merge: the right move when a conflict needs a conversation with whoever made the other change.
git config --global merge.conflictStyle zdiff3 (Git 2.35+) adds a section after ||||||| showing the lines as they were in the merge base, which makes it much easier to see what each side changed.
Keep conflicts small and rare: merge main into longer-running work often, keep branches short-lived, and talk before two people rework the same part of a file.

walkthrough.title: Make a conflict, and resolve it

steps.do: On a new branch, change - 300 ml milk to - 350 ml milk in pancakes.md and commit; then on main, change the same line to - 250 ml whole milk and commit.

steps.see: Merge branch 'more-milk' joining Use more milk for thinner pancakes and Use whole milk in pancakes.

lessons.title: Rebasing and tidying history
objectives: Explain what rebase does and how it differs from merge
Rebase a branch onto main
Tidy commits with interactive rebase, and know when not to rebase
key_points: git rebase main replays the current branch's commits, one by one, on top of the latest main. The result is a straight line of history, as if the work had started from today's main.

Rebased commits are new commits with new IDs, even when their changes are the same. So never rebase commits that others already have: rebase only your own work that hasn't been shared, or that only you use.
If a replayed commit conflicts, the rebase stops: resolve the file, git add it and run git rebase --continue; git rebase --abort puts the branch back as it was.

git rebase -i main opens a to-do list of the branch's commits. Change pick to reword to edit a message, to squash or fixup to fold a commit into the one above it (fixup discards its message), or to drop to remove it; lines can also be reordered.

Merging keeps the true history, with merge commits; rebasing gives a cleaner, linear history but rewrites commits. Many teams rebase their own branch to tidy it before review, then merge it through a pull request.

walkthrough.title: Rebase a branch, then squash its fix-up commits

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Creates cafe-menu/, a practice repository with branches to merge, rebase and tidy.
# Run it from the folder where you want cafe-menu to appear:  bash make_practice_repo.sh
set -euo pipefail
if [ -e cafe-menu ]; then
    echo "cafe-menu already exists here: delete it, or run this script in another folder." >&2
    exit 1
fi
if [ -z "$(git config user.name || true)" ] || [ -z "$(git config user.email || true)" ]; then
    echo 'Tell Git who you are first: git config --global user.name "Your Name"' >&2
    echo '                            git config --global user.email "you@example.com"' >&2
    exit 1
fi
git init -q -b main cafe-menu
cd cafe-menu
commit() { git add -A && git commit -q -m "$1"; }

cat > menu.md <<'EOF'
# Corner Café menu

## Opening hours

Monday to Friday, 8:00 to 16:00

## Soups

- Tomato soup ........ 4.50

## Mains

- Cheese toastie ..... 5.80
- Falafel wrap ....... 6.50
EOF
commit "Add the menu"
cat > menu.md <<'EOF'
# Corner Café menu

## Opening hours

Monday to Friday, 8:00 to 16:00

## Soups

- Tomato soup ........ 4.50
- Lentil soup ........ 4.20

## Mains

- Cheese toastie ..... 5.80
- Falafel wrap ....... 6.50
EOF
commit "Add lentil soup"

git switch -q -c feature/drinks
printf '\n## Drinks\n\n- Tea ................ 1.80\n- Coffee ............. 2.20\n' >> menu.md
commit "Add a drinks section"

git switch -q main
git switch -q -c feature/prices
sed -i.bak 's/^- Tomato soup ........ 4.50$/- Tomato soup ........ 4.80/' menu.md && rm menu.md.bak
commit "Raise the price of tomato soup"

git switch -q main
git switch -q -c feature/desserts
printf '# Desserts\n\n- Apple crumble ..... 3.90\n' > desserts.md
commit "Add a desserts page"
printf -- '- Choclate cake ..... 3.50\n' >> desserts.md
commit "WIP"
sed -i.bak 's/Choclate/Chocolate/' desserts.md && rm desserts.md.bak
commit "Fix typo"

git switch -q main
sed -i.bak 's/^- Tomato soup ........ 4.50$/- Roast tomato soup .. 4.50/' menu.md && rm menu.md.bak
commit "Rename tomato soup to roast tomato soup"

git switch -q -c fix/opening-hours
sed -i.bak 's/^Monday to Friday, 8:00 to 16:00$/Monday to Saturday, 8:00 to 16:00/' menu.md && rm menu.md.bak
commit "Open on Saturdays"

git switch -q main
echo "Created cafe-menu with branches: $(git branch --format='%(refname:short)' | tr '\n' ' ')"

modules.title: Remotes and GitHub
modules.summary: Share work through remotes: clone, fetch, pull and push, recover from a rejected push, share branches with teammates, and connect to GitHub with HTTPS or SSH, publish repositories and work with forks.

lessons.title: Remotes: clone, fetch, pull and push
objectives: Explain remotes and remote-tracking branches
Clone, fetch, pull and push
Recover from a rejected push
key_points: A remote is another copy of the repository that you exchange commits with, usually on a server such as GitHub. git clone URL copies a repository and names its source origin; git remote -v lists the remotes.
Remote-tracking branches such as origin/main record where the remote's branches were when you last talked to it. git fetch updates them without touching your own branches, so it's always safe.

git pull is git fetch followed by integrating origin's branch into yours, by merging or rebasing. If both sides have new commits and no choice is configured, Git stops with fatal: Need to specify how to reconcile divergent branches.

git push sends your commits to the remote; git push -u origin main also sets the upstream, so later a plain git push or git pull knows where to go. git branch -vv shows each branch's upstream and whether it's ahead or behind.

A push is rejected (fetch first) when the remote has commits you don't: fetch, integrate them with git pull --rebase or a merge, and push again. Never force-push a shared branch; for your own pushed branch, --force-with-lease is the safer force.

Set a default for pulls once: git config --global pull.rebase true rebases your local commits on top of the remote's (a straight history); false merges instead, and pull.ff only refuses anything but a fast-forward.

walkthrough.title: Two people, one remote, on one computer

steps.do: Make a bare repository to act as the shared server: it has history but no working files.
steps.code:
cd ..
git init --bare shared.git
steps.see: Initialized empty Git repository in .../shared.git/

steps.do: Connect the recipes repository to it and push main, setting the upstream.
steps.code:
cd recipes
git remote add origin ../shared.git
git push -u origin main
git remote -v
steps.see: * [new branch]      main -> main and branch 'main' set up to track 'origin/main'.

steps.do: Play a second person: clone the remote into another folder, give that clone its own author, and push a commit.
steps.code:
cd ..
git clone shared.git recipes-ben
cd recipes-ben
git config user.name "Ben Okafor"
git config user.email "ben@example.com"
printf '# Shopping list\n\n- flour\n- eggs\n' > shopping.md
git add shopping.md
git commit -m "Add a shopping list"
git push
steps.see: Cloning into 'recipes-ben'... done. and a push ending main -> main.

steps.do: Back in recipes, commit something else and try to push.
steps.code:
cd ../recipes
printf '\nOven temperatures are for a fan oven.\n' >> README.md
git commit -am "Say which oven the temperatures are for"
git push
steps.see: ! [rejected]        main -> main (fetch first): the remote has Ben's commit, which you don't.

steps.do: Fetch, and see how the branches stand.
steps.code:
git fetch
git status
steps.see: Your branch and 'origin/main' have diverged, and have 1 and 1 different commits each, respectively.

steps.do: Try a plain pull.
steps.code: git pull
steps.see: hint: You have divergent branches and need to specify how to reconcile them. ... fatal: Need to specify how to reconcile divergent branches.

steps.do: Rebase your commit on top of Ben's, push, and check the upstream status.
steps.code:
git pull --rebase
git push
git branch -vv
steps.see: Successfully rebased and updated refs/heads/main., then a successful push, then * main ... [origin/main] Say which oven the temperatures are for.

steps.do: Choose a default for future pulls, so Git doesn't ask again.
steps.code: git config --global pull.rebase true

lessons.title: GitHub: access, repositories and forks
objectives: Authenticate to GitHub over HTTPS or SSH
Publish a local repository on GitHub
Contribute to another project through a fork
key_points: GitHub hosts Git repositories and adds collaboration around them: pull requests, reviews, issues and access control. Your local Git talks to it like any other remote, over HTTPS or SSH.

GitHub doesn't accept your account password for Git over HTTPS. Use a credential manager (Git for Windows includes Git Credential Manager), a personal access token, or the GitHub CLI's gh auth login, which can set Git up for you.

For SSH, create a key pair with ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "you@example.com", add the public key (the .pub file) to your GitHub account's SSH keys, and test with ssh -T git@github.com. Never share the private key.

To publish an existing repository, create an empty one on GitHub (without a README, so the histories don't clash), add it as a remote and push with -u. gh repo create name --public --source=. --push does it in one step.

Team members with write access push branches to the shared repository. To contribute to a project you can't push to, fork it (your own copy on GitHub), clone your fork, and open pull requests from it.

Keep a fork up to date by adding the original as a second remote, git remote add upstream URL, then git fetch upstream and merging upstream/main into your main; GitHub's Sync fork button does the same.

walkthrough.title: Connect to GitHub and publish a repository

steps.do: Install the GitHub CLI (cli.github.com) and log in. Choose GitHub.com and HTTPS, and let it authenticate Git with your GitHub credentials.
steps.code:
gh auth login
gh auth status
steps.see: gh auth status reports that you're logged in to github.com.

steps.do: Or use SSH: create a key, then paste the public key into GitHub under Settings, SSH and GPG keys, New SSH key.
steps.code:
ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "you@example.com"
cat ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub
steps.see: One line starting ssh-ed25519: the public half, safe to share.

steps.do: Test the SSH connection.
steps.code: ssh -T git@github.com
steps.see: Hi YOUR-NAME! You've successfully authenticated, but GitHub does not provide shell access.

steps.do: Publish the recipes repository: from inside its folder, create it on GitHub and push it in one step. It already has a remote called origin (the local shared.git), so name this one github.
steps.code: gh repo create recipes --public --source=. --remote=github --push
steps.see: Your repository on github.com, with the whole history.

steps.do: Or do it by hand: on github.com choose New repository, leave it empty (no README), then add it as a remote and push.
steps.code:
git remote add github https://github.com/YOUR-NAME/recipes.git
git push -u github main

steps.do: To contribute to someone else's project, click Fork on its GitHub page, then clone your fork and add the original as upstream.
steps.code:
git clone https://github.com/YOUR-NAME/PROJECT.git
cd PROJECT
git remote add upstream https://github.com/OWNER/PROJECT.git
git fetch upstream
git merge upstream/main

lessons.title: Working on shared branches
objectives: Push a branch and set its upstream
Pick up a teammate's branch and add to it
Clean up remote branches after merging
key_points: Push a feature branch early with git push -u origin name, so teammates can see it and it's backed up; after that, git push and git pull on the branch need no arguments.
After git fetch, a teammate's branch appears as origin/name. git switch name then creates a local branch that tracks it, and commits you push from it go to the same branch on the remote.
A branch shared by two people needs the same care as main: pull before you push, and don't rewrite its history with a rebase or a force-push without agreeing it first.

Delete a remote branch once it's merged with git push origin --delete name. Other clones keep their origin/name until they run git fetch --prune (or set fetch.prune to true), which removes tracking branches that no longer exist.
git branch -r lists remote-tracking branches, git branch -a lists everything, and git log --oneline --graph --all shows how local and remote branches relate.

walkthrough.title: Share a branch with a teammate

steps.do: In recipes, start a branch, commit, and push it with an upstream.
steps.code:
git switch -c add-smoothies
printf '# Smoothies\n\n- banana and oat\n' > smoothies.md
git add smoothies.md
git commit -m "Add a smoothie recipe"
git push -u origin add-smoothies
steps.see: * [new branch]      add-smoothies -> add-smoothies and branch 'add-smoothies' set up to track 'origin/add-smoothies'.

steps.do: In Ben's clone, fetch and list the remote branches.
steps.code:
cd ../recipes-ben
git fetch
git branch -r
steps.see: * [new branch]      add-smoothies -> origin/add-smoothies, then origin/HEAD -> origin/main, origin/add-smoothies and origin/main.

steps.do: Switch to the branch, which creates a local branch tracking it; add a recipe and push.
steps.code:
git switch add-smoothies
printf -- '- mango and lime\n' >> smoothies.md
git commit -am "Add a mango smoothie"
git push
steps.see: branch 'add-smoothies' set up to track 'origin/add-smoothies'.

steps.do: Back in recipes, pull Ben's commit, merge the branch into main and push.
steps.code:
cd ../recipes
git pull
git switch main
git merge add-smoothies
git push
steps.see: A Fast-forward for the branch, then another for main.

steps.do: Delete the branch on the remote, then tidy Ben's clone.
steps.code:
git push origin --delete add-smoothies
cd ../recipes-ben
git fetch --prune
git switch main
git pull
git branch -d add-smoothies
steps.see: - [deleted]         add-smoothies, then - [deleted]         (none)     -> origin/add-smoothies from the prune.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Creates a shared remote (team.git) and two clones of it, ana/ and ben/, for two team members.
# Run it from an empty folder:  bash make_team.sh
set -euo pipefail
for d in team.git ana ben; do
    if [ -e "$d" ]; then echo "$d already exists here: run this script in an empty folder." >&2; exit 1; fi
done
git init -q --bare -b main team.git
git clone -q team.git ana 2>/dev/null
cd ana
git config user.name "Ana Costa"
git config user.email "ana@example.com"
printf '# Team handbook\n\nHow our team works together.\n' > README.md
git add README.md
git commit -q -m "Start the team handbook"
git push -q -u origin main
cd ..
git clone -q team.git ben
cd ben
git config user.name "Ben Okafor"
git config user.email "ben@example.com"
cd ..
echo "Created team.git (the shared remote) and two clones of it: ana/ and ben/."

hints: Each clone has its own author name, set by the script, so the history shows who made each commit: try git log --format='%h %an %s'.
If git pull complains about divergent branches, you ran it without --rebase: run git pull --rebase, or set git config --global pull.rebase true.
Lost track? git status in each clone says which branch you're on and whether it's ahead of or behind origin.

modules.title: Pull requests, reviews and releases
modules.summary: Work as a team on GitHub: propose changes in pull requests, review them well, choose a workflow and a merge method, protect main, and mark releases with tags and GitHub Releases.

lessons.title: Pull requests
objectives: Explain what a pull request is for
Open a pull request from GitHub or the GitHub CLI
Link issues and use a template so pull requests are easy to review
key_points: A pull request (PR) asks to merge one branch into another, usually a feature branch into main. It shows the commits and the combined changes, and it's where the team discusses, reviews and checks the work before it's merged.
Open one after pushing a branch, from the Compare & pull request banner on GitHub or with gh pr create. Give it a clear title and a description of what changed, why, and how it was tested.

Pushing more commits to the branch updates the open pull request, so review feedback is answered with new commits. A draft pull request (gh pr create --draft) shares work in progress without asking for a review yet.
Writing Closes #12 (or Fixes #12) in a pull request's description links issue 12 and closes it automatically when the pull request is merged into the default branch.
A file at .github/pull_request_template.md pre-fills the description of every new pull request, for example with headings for what, why and testing, so authors don't forget them.
Small pull requests get faster, better reviews: aim for one focused change that a reviewer can read in one sitting, and split big features into a series of pull requests.

steps.do: Create an issue for the work, so the pull request can close it.
steps.code: gh issue create --title "Add a recipe index" --body "README.md should list every recipe."
steps.see: The new issue's URL, ending in /issues/1 in a new repository.

steps.do: Make the change on a branch and push it to GitHub (the remote called github in the last module).
steps.code:
git switch -c recipe-index
# ...add the list of recipes to README.md...
git commit -am "Add a recipe index to the README"
git push -u github recipe-index

steps.do: Open the pull request: GitHub's repository page offers Compare & pull request for a recently pushed branch, or use the GitHub CLI.
steps.code: gh pr create --title "Add a recipe index to the README" --body "Lists every recipe. Closes #1"
steps.see: The pull request's URL, ending in /pull/2: issues and pull requests share one numbering.

steps.do: Open it in the browser and look at its Conversation, Commits and Files changed tabs.
steps.code: gh pr view --web

steps.do: Push one more commit to the branch, then refresh the page: the pull request has updated itself.
steps.code:
git commit -am "Link each recipe in the index"
git push

steps.do: For future pull requests, add a template on main as .github/pull_request_template.md.
steps.code:
## What

<!-- What does this pull request change? -->

## Why

<!-- Why is the change needed? Link the issue it closes, for example: Closes #12 -->

## How it was tested

<!-- What did you check, and how? -->

lessons.title: Code review
objectives: Review a pull request with comments and suggestions, then approve or request changes
Respond to review feedback as the author
Use CODEOWNERS and branch protection to get the right reviews
key_points: A review checks that a change is correct, readable, tested and fits the design, and it spreads knowledge of the code across the team. Review the change, not the person: be specific and kind, and explain why.
On the Files changed tab, comment on a line or a range of lines and start a review. A suggestion block proposes exact replacement lines, which the author can apply with Commit suggestion.
Submitting a review means choosing Comment (feedback only), Approve, or Request changes, which blocks merging when approvals are required. Authors can't approve their own pull requests.

As the author, answer each comment, push follow-up commits, mark conversations resolved, and re-request review when ready. gh pr checkout 12 fetches pull request 12's branch so you can run it locally.
A CODEOWNERS file (in .github/, the repository root or docs/) maps paths to people or teams, such as docs/ @maria; GitHub then requests their review on any pull request that touches those paths.

Branch protection rules and rulesets, in the repository's settings, can require a pull request, a number of approvals, code owners' review and passing status checks before merging into main, and can block force pushes.

steps.do: Fetch the pull request's branch locally and try the change.
steps.code:
gh pr checkout 2
cat README.md
steps.see: You're on the pull request's branch, with the recipe index in README.md.

steps.do: On GitHub, open the pull request's Files changed tab. Hover over a line, click the + that appears, and write a comment; choose Start a review to collect several comments into one review.
To propose an exact change, add a suggestion block to a comment (the suggestion button in the comment box inserts one) and edit the line inside it.
steps.code:
```suggestion
- [Pancakes](pancakes.md): the family favourite
```

steps.do: Finish the review: open the review panel on the Files changed tab, write a summary, choose Comment, Approve or Request changes, and submit. gh pr review does the same from the terminal.
steps.code:
gh pr review 2 --request-changes --body "Nice index. One suggestion inline."
gh pr review 2 --approve

steps.do: As the author, click Commit suggestion on the suggestion, reply to the other comments and resolve them, then pull the new commit into your local branch.
steps.code: git pull

steps.do: Ask for reviews automatically: on main, add .github/CODEOWNERS naming who owns which files (later lines take precedence).
steps.code:
# Everything needs a review from the maintainer
*          @YOUR-NAME
# The pancake recipe also needs its cook
pancakes.md @A-TEAMMATE

lessons.title: Team workflows and merge methods
objectives: Compare GitHub flow, trunk-based development and Git flow
Choose between merge commits, squash merging and rebase merging
Match a workflow to the way a team releases
key_points: GitHub flow: main is always releasable; each change starts as a branch from main, goes through a pull request with review and checks, is merged, then deployed. It's simple and suits teams that release continuously.

Trunk-based development: everyone integrates into main (the trunk) at least daily, through very short-lived branches or small direct commits, with unfinished features hidden behind feature flags. It needs good automated tests, and keeps every merge small.

Git flow: long-lived main and develop branches, plus feature, release and hotfix branches. It suits software shipped in numbered versions on a schedule, such as installed apps, but adds ceremony and long-lived branches that drift apart.

GitHub's merge button has three methods: Create a merge commit keeps every commit plus a merge; Squash and merge makes the pull request one commit on main, titled with its number, such as (#2); Rebase and merge replays the commits onto main without a merge commit.
Teams usually allow one merge method, in the repository's settings, so history stays consistent, and turn on automatically deleting head branches, so merged branches disappear.

Choose by how you release: continuous deployment fits GitHub flow or trunk-based development, while supporting several released versions needs release branches, such as release/1.4, that receive fixes with git cherry-pick.

walkthrough.title: See the three merge methods' results locally

steps.do: In a throwaway clone of recipes, make a branch with two commits.
steps.code:
cd ..
git clone -q recipes methods
cd methods
git switch -c add-porridge
# ...commit Add a porridge recipe, then Add porridge toppings...
git switch main

steps.do: Merge commit: what Create a merge commit does.
steps.code:
git merge --no-ff --no-edit add-porridge
git log --oneline --graph -4
steps.see: *   a663094 Merge branch 'add-porridge' above the branch's two commits.

steps.do: Undo that merge (fine in a throwaway clone), then squash: all the branch's changes staged as one commit, which you then make yourself.
steps.code:
git reset --hard HEAD~1
git merge --squash add-porridge
git commit -m "Add a porridge recipe (#3)"
git log --oneline --graph -3
steps.see: Squash commit -- not updating HEAD, then a single commit, Add a porridge recipe (#3), on top of main: what Squash and merge produces.

steps.do: Undo it again, then rebase and fast-forward: the branch's commits land on main as they are, with no merge commit.
steps.code:
git reset --hard HEAD~1
git switch add-porridge
git rebase main
git switch main
git merge --ff-only add-porridge
git log --oneline --graph -3
steps.see: Add porridge toppings and Add a porridge recipe in a straight line on main: what Rebase and merge produces.

steps.do: On GitHub, see which methods a repository allows: Settings, General, Pull Requests. Leave the one your team chooses ticked, and tick Automatically delete head branches.

lessons.title: Tags and releases
objectives: Mark releases with annotated tags and semantic version numbers
Push tags and publish a GitHub Release
Patch an older release on a release branch with cherry-pick
key_points: A tag is a fixed name for one commit, used to mark releases. An annotated tag (git tag -a v1.2.0 -m "message") is a full object with a tagger, date and message; a lightweight tag (git tag v1.2.0) is just a name, best for private or temporary marks.

Semantic versioning numbers releases MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH: increase PATCH for bug fixes, MINOR for new features that keep compatibility, and MAJOR for changes that break it, so 1.4.2 is followed by 1.4.3, 1.5.0 or 2.0.0.

git push doesn't send tags. Push one with git push origin v1.2.0, or use git push --follow-tags to send the annotated tags on the commits being pushed. git describe --tags names a commit by the nearest tag, as in v1.0.0-1-g17a9805.

A GitHub Release is built on a tag and adds release notes and downloadable files. gh release create v1.2.0 --generate-notes publishes one, with notes listing the pull requests merged since the previous release.

To fix an older release, branch from its tag (git switch -c release/1.0 v1.0.0), copy the fix from main with git cherry-pick <commit>, which applies its change as a new commit, and tag the result v1.0.1.

steps.do: Tag the current commit as the first release, and list tags with their messages.
steps.code:
git tag -a v1.0.0 -m "First release: five tested recipes"
git tag -n
steps.see: v1.0.0          First release: five tested recipes

steps.do: Look at the tag object: it has its own tagger, date and message.
steps.code: git show v1.0.0 --no-patch
steps.see: tag v1.0.0, Tagger: Sam Taylor <sam@example.com>, the message, then the commit it marks.

steps.do: Push the tag: tags don't travel with a plain git push.
steps.code: git push origin v1.0.0

steps.do: Commit something new, then ask Git to describe where you are.
steps.code:
printf '\nAll recipes use metric measures.\n' >> README.md
git commit -am "Say that recipes use metric measures"
git describe --tags
steps.see: v1.0.0-1-g17a9805: one commit after v1.0.0, and that commit's short hash after the g.

steps.do: People on 1.0 need a fix. Make a release branch from the tag; fix the cooking time on main and commit; then copy the fix across with cherry-pick.
steps.code:
git switch -c release/1.0 v1.0.0
git switch main
# ...fix the cooking time in pancakes.md...
git commit -am "Fix the cooking time in pancakes"
git switch release/1.0
git cherry-pick main
steps.see: [release/1.0 2b816a2] Fix the cooking time in pancakes: the same change, as a new commit.

steps.do: Tag the patch release and push the branch with its annotated tags.
steps.code:
git tag -a v1.0.1 -m "Fix the cooking time in pancakes"

## Commits

## Reviews

## Merging

modules.title: Ignore, undo and automate
modules.summary: Keep the wrong files out with .gitignore, undo almost anything with restore, reset, revert and the reflog, and automate checks with Git hooks that the whole team shares.

lessons.title: .gitignore: keep the right files out
objectives: Write .gitignore patterns, including exceptions
Find which rule ignores a file
Stop tracking a committed file, and handle a committed secret
key_points: A .gitignore file lists patterns for files Git should leave untracked: *.log matches any .log file, build/ matches a folder, a leading / anchors a pattern to the .gitignore's own folder, and **/ matches folders at any depth.

A pattern starting with ! makes an exception, so *.log followed by !keep.log ignores every log except keep.log. Lines starting with # are comments, and a .gitignore in a sub-folder applies within that folder.
Commit .gitignore so the whole team shares it. Keep personal clutter, such as editor and operating-system files, in a global ignore file: git config --global core.excludesFile ~/.gitignore_global.
git status --ignored lists ignored files, and git check-ignore -v file names the .gitignore line that matches it: the quickest way to debug a rule.
Ignoring doesn't affect files Git already tracks. To stop tracking one, add it to .gitignore and run git rm --cached file, which removes it from the repository but leaves it on disk.
If a secret such as a password or API key was ever committed, treat it as leaked: revoke it and issue a new one. Deleting it in a later commit leaves it in the history, and copies may already exist.

steps.do: Create files that shouldn't be committed (a log, local settings and build output) and one example log that should.
steps.code:
printf 'API_KEY=not-a-real-key\n' > .env
printf 'started\n' > debug.log
printf 'example\n' > keep.log
mkdir -p build
printf 'x\n' > build/output.txt

steps.do: Write .gitignore.
steps.code:
# Logs, except the example log
*.log
!keep.log

# Build output and local settings
build/
.env

steps.do: Compare the normal status with the ignored files shown.
steps.code:
git status --short
git status --short --ignored
steps.see: ?? .gitignore and ?? keep.log; with --ignored, also !! .env, !! build/ and !! debug.log.

steps.do: Ask which rule matches each file.
steps.code: git check-ignore -v debug.log build/output.txt .env keep.log
steps.see: .gitignore:2:*.log debug.log, .gitignore:6:build/ build/output.txt, .gitignore:7:.env .env and .gitignore:3:!keep.log keep.log, the exception.

steps.do: Commit the rules and the example log.
steps.code:
git add .gitignore keep.log
git commit -m "Ignore logs, build output and local settings"

steps.do: Now a file committed by mistake: commit settings.local, then add it to .gitignore.
steps.code:
printf 'theme=dark\n' > settings.local
git add settings.local
git commit -m "Add local settings"
printf 'settings.local\n' >> .gitignore
git status --short
steps.see: Only  M .gitignore: the new rule doesn't stop Git tracking a file it already has.

steps.do: Stop tracking it, but keep it on disk, and commit.
steps.code:
git rm --cached settings.local
git commit -am "Stop tracking settings.local"
git status --short --ignored
steps.see: rm 'settings.local', then delete mode 100644 settings.local in the commit, and !! settings.local among the ignored files.

lessons.title: Undoing changes: restore, reset, revert and the reflog
objectives: Discard or unstage changes with git restore
Undo commits with reset or revert, and choose between them
Recover lost commits with the reflog, and park work with git stash
key_points: git restore file throws away uncommitted changes to a file, returning it to the last commit; git restore --staged file unstages it but keeps the changes. Discarded changes that were never committed can't be recovered.
git reset moves the current branch back: --soft HEAD~1 undoes the last commit but keeps its changes staged; the default, --mixed, keeps them unstaged; --hard also discards them from the working tree.
git revert <commit> makes a new commit that undoes an earlier one, without rewriting history. Use revert for commits that have been pushed or shared, and reset only for commits nobody else has.

The reflog (git reflog) records every position HEAD has had, even after a reset. To recover a commit that seems lost, find it in the reflog and put a branch on it, such as git branch rescued HEAD@{1}.
git stash puts uncommitted changes aside and cleans the working tree, so you can switch branches; git stash list shows what's stored, and git stash pop brings the latest back.
Choose the gentlest tool: restore for files, --amend for the last unpushed commit, revert for anything shared, reset --hard only when you're sure, and the reflog when something has gone wrong.

steps.do: Make a change, then discard it.
steps.code:
printf -- '- a pinch of chilli\n' >> pancakes.md
git status --short
git restore pancakes.md
git status --short
steps.see: M pancakes.md, then nothing: the change is gone for good.

steps.do: Stage a change, then unstage it.
steps.code:
printf -- '- a pinch of chilli\n' >> pancakes.md
git add pancakes.md
git restore --staged pancakes.md
git status --short
steps.see: M pancakes.md: still changed, but no longer staged.

steps.do: Commit it, then undo the commit but keep the change staged.
steps.code:
git commit -am "Add chilli to pancakes"
git reset --soft HEAD~1
git status --short
steps.see: M  pancakes.md: staged again, and the commit is gone from the branch.

steps.do: Commit it again. This time suppose it was already pushed, and undo it with a new commit.
steps.code:
git commit -m "Add chilli to pancakes"
git revert --no-edit HEAD
git log --oneline -3
steps.see: Revert "Add chilli to pancakes" on top of Add chilli to pancakes: both stay in the history.

steps.do: Lose a commit on purpose with a hard reset.
steps.code:
printf '
## Variations

Add grated apple to the batter.
' >> pancakes.md
git commit -am "Add an apple variation"
git reset --hard HEAD~1
steps.see: HEAD is now at b023bcb Revert "Add chilli to pancakes"

steps.do: Find it in the reflog, and rescue it.
steps.code:
git reflog -4
git branch rescued HEAD@{1}
git merge rescued
git branch -d rescued
steps.see: HEAD@{1}: commit: Add an apple variation in the reflog, then a Fast-forward that brings the commit back.

steps.do: Park unfinished work with stash, and bring it back.
steps.code:
printf '\nHalf-finished idea.\n' >> README.md
git stash
git stash list
git stash pop
steps.see: Saved working directory and index state WIP on main: ..., then stash@{0}: WIP on main: ..., then the change back in README.md.

lessons.title: Automating checks with Git hooks
objectives: Explain what Git hooks are and when they run
Write pre-commit and commit-msg hooks
Share hooks with a team, and know their limits
key_points: Hooks are scripts that Git runs at certain moments: pre-commit before a commit is made, commit-msg to check the message, pre-push before a push. If a hook exits with a non-zero status, Git stops the operation.
Hooks live in .git/hooks, named exactly after the event (pre-commit, with no extension), and must be executable on macOS and Linux (chmod +x). Git for Windows runs them with the shell it includes.
A commit-msg hook receives the path of a file holding the message as its first argument ($1), so it can read the summary line and reject messages that are too short or badly formatted.

The .git folder isn't committed, so hooks in it aren't shared. Commit them in a folder such as .githooks and have each person run git config core.hooksPath .githooks, which replaces .git/hooks entirely.
Frameworks such as pre-commit (pre-commit.com) install and run shared hooks from a configuration file, with ready-made checks for formatting, linting and secrets.

Hooks run on each person's computer and git commit --no-verify skips them, so they're a convenience, not a guarantee: enforce important rules on the server too, with branch protection and required checks.

steps.do: Write a pre-commit hook that refuses staged changes containing API_KEY=, save it as .git/hooks/pre-commit, and make it executable with chmod +x .git/hooks/pre-commit.
steps.code:
#!/bin/sh
# pre-commit: refuse to commit anything that looks like a secret.
if git diff --cached | grep -q "API_KEY="; then
    echo "pre-commit: the staged changes contain API_KEY=; take the secret out and use .env instead." >&2
    exit 1
fi

steps.do: Try to commit a file with a key in it.
steps.code:
printf 'API_KEY=not-a-real-key\n' > config.txt
git add config.txt
git commit -m "Add the configuration"
steps.see: pre-commit: the staged changes contain API_KEY=; take the secret out and use .env instead. No commit is made.

steps.do: Unstage the file and delete it.
steps.code:
git restore --staged config.txt
rm config.txt

steps.do: Write a commit-msg hook in a .githooks folder, where it can be committed and shared: save it as .githooks/commit-msg.
steps.code:
#!/bin/sh
# commit-msg: Git passes the path of the file holding the message as $1.
summary=$(head -n 1 "$1")
if [ ${#summary} -lt 10 ]; then
    echo "commit-msg: the summary line is too short; describe the change in at least 10 characters." >&2
    exit 1
fi

steps.do: Make it executable and point Git at the folder. From now on .git/hooks is ignored, so the pre-commit hook no longer runs unless you move it into .githooks too.
steps.code:
chmod +x .githooks/commit-msg
git config core.hooksPath .githooks

steps.do: Try a lazy message, then a good one.
steps.code:
printf '\nRecipes are tested twice.\n' >> README.md
git commit -am "wip"
git commit -am "Say that recipes are tested twice"
steps.see: commit-msg: the summary line is too short; describe the change in at least 10 characters. Then the second commit goes through.

steps.do: Commit the hook so teammates get it; each of them runs the same git config core.hooksPath command once.
steps.code:
git add .githooks
git commit -m "Share the commit-msg hook in .githooks"

lab.title: Put a messy repository right
lab.goal: Repair a repository without losing anything: recover a commit lost in a hard reset, revert a bad commit that was shared, stop tracking files that should never have been committed, and add a shared commit-msg hook.
setup: Git 2.28 or later, configured with your name and email
The starter files make_messy_repo.sh and commit-msg in one folder (on Windows, use Git Bash)

steps.do: Create the repository and read its history.
steps.code:
bash make_messy_repo.sh
cd notes-app
git log --oneline
steps.see: Four commits, the newest being Change the default colour to neon green.

steps.do: A commit called Add export to CSV was lost in a hard reset. Find it in the reflog.
steps.code: git reflog
steps.see: A line ending HEAD@{1}: commit: Add export to CSV.

steps.do: Bring it back: put a branch on it and merge that into main.
steps.see: Fast-forward, and the export_csv function back in notes.py.

steps.do: The neon green change was shared, so don't rewrite history: revert it, using its hash from git log --oneline.
steps.code:
git log --oneline
git revert --no-edit <hash>
cat theme.py
steps.see: [main ...] Revert "Change the default colour to neon green", and colour = "white" in theme.py.

steps.do: Stop tracking .env and debug.log: ignore them, take them out of the repository but not off the disk, and commit.
steps.code:
printf '.env\n*.log\n' > .gitignore
git rm --cached .env debug.log
git add .gitignore
git commit -m "Stop tracking local settings and logs"
git check-ignore -v .env debug.log
steps.see: rm '.env' and rm 'debug.log', then .gitignore:1:.env .env and .gitignore:2:*.log debug.log.

steps.do: The .env file is still in an older commit. Write one sentence on what you'd do if its API_KEY had been real.
Install the shared commit-msg hook from the starter files.
steps.code:
mkdir .githooks
cp ../commit-msg .githooks/
chmod +x .githooks/commit-msg
git config core.hooksPath .githooks

steps.do: Add a count function to notes.py, then try three commit messages.
steps.code:
printf '

def count(notes):
    return len(notes)
' >> notes.py
git commit -am "wip"
git commit -am "add a count function"
git commit -am "Add a function that counts the notes"
steps.see: Two refusals from commit-msg (the summary is too short; start it with a capital letter), then the commit.

steps.do: Commit the hook and check that everything is committed.
steps.code:
git add .githooks
git commit -m "Share a commit-msg hook in .githooks"
git log --oneline
git status
steps.see: Nine commits, and nothing to commit, working tree clean.

checks.text: The lost commit was recovered from the reflog.
look_for: HEAD@{1}: commit: Add export to CSV

checks.text: The bad commit was undone with a revert, not removed from history.
look_for: Revert "Change the default colour to neon green"

checks.text: .env and debug.log are ignored and no longer tracked.
The hook rejects a short message and a lower-case one, and accepts a good one.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Creates notes-app/, a repository with some mistakes in its history for you to put right.
# Run it from the folder where you want notes-app to appear:  bash make_messy_repo.sh
set -euo pipefail
if [ -e notes-app ]; then
    echo "notes-app already exists here: delete it, or run this script in another folder." >&2
    exit 1
fi
if [ -z "$(git config user.name || true)" ]; then
    echo 'Tell Git who you are first: git config --global user.name "Your Name"' >&2
    exit 1
fi
git init -q -b main notes-app
cd notes-app
commit() { git add -A && git commit -q -m "$1"; }

printf 'def add_note(notes, text):\n    notes.append(text)\n    return notes\n' > notes.py
printf 'colour = "white"\n' > theme.py
commit "Add the notes app"

printf 'API_KEY=not-a-real-key\n' > .env
printf 'starting notes app\n' > debug.log
commit "Add local settings"

printf 'def dark_mode():\n    return {"background": "black", "text": "white"}\n' >> theme.py
commit "Add dark mode"

sed -i.bak 's/^colour = "white"$/colour = "neon green"/' theme.py && rm theme.py.bak
commit "Change the default colour to neon green"

printf '\n\ndef export_csv(notes):\n    return "\\n".join(notes)\n' >> notes.py
commit "Add export to CSV"
git reset -q --hard HEAD~1          # oops: the export commit is no longer on main

echo "Created notes-app. Its history needs some care: see the lab steps."

#!/bin/sh
# commit-msg hook: Git runs it with the path of the file that holds the commit message.
# A non-zero exit status stops the commit.
summary=$(head -n 1 "$1")
length=${#summary}

if [ "$length" -lt 10 ]; then
    echo "commit-msg: the summary line has $length characters; describe the change in at least 10." >&2
    exit 1
fi
if [ "$length" -gt 72 ]; then
    echo "commit-msg: the summary line has $length characters; keep it to 72 or fewer." >&2
    exit 1
fi
case "$summary" in
    [[:lower:]]*)
        echo "commit-msg: start the summary line with a capital letter." >&2
        exit 1
        ;;
esac
exit 0

hints: HEAD@{1} means where HEAD was one move ago. If you've run other commands since, the lost commit has a higher number: look for its message in git reflog.
If the hook doesn't run, check git config core.hooksPath and that the file is called exactly commit-msg, with no extension, and is executable.
git revert opens your editor for the message unless you pass --no-edit.

project.title: Run a team project on GitHub, from first commit to release
project.brief: Set up and run a small project the way a professional team would, on GitHub. Choose something small to build or write, such as a recipe collection, a study guide or a short script. Work with a partner if you can, each with your own account, or alone with two clones of your own. Write a CONTRIBUTING.md that describes your workflow (GitHub flow or trunk-based development, branch names, commit message rules, how reviews work and which merge method you use), and add a .gitignore, a pull request template, a CODEOWNERS file and a commit-msg hook shared through core.hooksPath. Protect main so changes need a pull request. Then do the work through issues and at least three pull requests: one that resolves a merge conflict, one tidied with an interactive rebase before review, and one improved in response to review comments. Finish by tagging v1.0.0 with an annotated tag, publishing a GitHub Release with notes, and making a v1.0.1 patch on a release branch with a cherry-picked fix.
deliverables: The repository's URL, with README.md, CONTRIBUTING.md, .gitignore, a pull request template, CODEOWNERS and the shared hook
A rule or ruleset on main that requires a pull request (a screenshot or a description of its settings)
Links to at least three merged pull requests, each closing an issue, with the review discussion visible
The output of git log --oneline --graph --all, showing the history and the release branch
Annotated tags v1.0.0 and v1.0.1, and the GitHub Release for v1.0.0
A short reflection, about half a page: what went wrong, how you recovered, and what you'd change in your workflow

rubric.name: Repository set-up
rubric.description: README, a CONTRIBUTING.md with a clear and consistent workflow, a .gitignore that fits the project, a pull request template, CODEOWNERS and a working shared hook.

rubric.name: Branches and pull requests
rubric.description: Every change arrives through a focused pull request linked to an issue, with a description that follows the template; the conflict and the interactive rebase are handled correctly.

rubric.name: Code review
rubric.description: Reviews contain specific, kind comments and at least one suggestion; the author responds with follow-up commits and resolves the conversations.

rubric.name: History quality
rubric.description: Small commits with clear summary lines and bodies where needed, no WIP or fix-up commits left on main, and one merge method used consistently.

rubric.name: Releases
rubric.description: Annotated, semantically versioned tags, a GitHub Release with notes, and v1.0.1 made on a release branch with a cherry-picked fix.

rubric.name: Reflection
rubric.description: An honest account of the problems met and how Git was used to recover, with sensible changes to the workflow.
